title: Is there treasure on Oak Island?
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explore the Oak Island treasure legend off Nova Scotia, from Daniel McGinnis's 1795 discovery of a pulley block and the "money pit," through flooding, the coconut fiber and the five-finger drain, legends (pirates, Knights Templar, Freemasons, Marie Antoinette, Francis Bacon), the many expeditions (Onslow, Truro, Eldorado, Dunfield, Triton Alliance with Blankenship and Tobias, Nolan's Cross), and the skeptic versus believer debate. The episode ends with listener mail from JB about poison ivy smoke from burned logs.

segments.title: Opening banter and Oak Island introduction
segments.summary: Hosts riff on a Nova Scotia accent and TV shows, then introduce Oak Island as a frequently requested topic, a small divisive island of about 140 acres off Nova Scotia that draws believers, treasure hunters and skeptics.

segments.title: Mildred Restall and the Oak Island curse
segments.summary: Discussion of Mildred Restall's 1965 article and her and husband Robert's 1959 move to Oak Island to hunt treasure, after their circus motorcycle globe act. The hosts note the curse is mostly a TV creation rather than an early belief.

segments.title: Daniel McGinnis's discovery and the money pit
segments.summary: Sixteen-year-old Daniel McGinnis found a pulley block on an oak tree and a cleared depression. He and friends dug about ten feet and hit an oak log platform, with more platforms supposedly every ten feet, creating the money pit. They stopped and needed bigger equipment and funding.

segments.title: Pirate burial theories and the Onslow company dig
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why pirates buried treasure. The pit was refilled and nine years later the Onslow Company funded a return. They found coconut fiber and charcoal that should not be on the island, and a legendary cipher stone reportedly reading about two million pounds buried forty feet below, which no one has documented.

segments.title: Flooding of the pit
segments.summary: Near one hundred feet the pit flooded with water overnight. Efforts to bail failed, and the Onslow expedition gave up when funding ran out. Believers suspect a booby trap while skeptics point to natural seawater and underground channels.

segments.title: Truro Company and the five finger drain
segments.summary: In 1849 the Truro Company dug again and met the same flooding. They searched the shoreline and found a stone drainage system, the five finger drain, about 145 feet wide and tied to tide height, with coconut fiber used as a filter. Believers see a trap, skeptics see Freemason activity or similar.

segments.title: Legends of what is buried: Templars, Freemasons, Marie Antoinette, Francis Bacon
segments.summary: The hosts run through legends: Knights Templar treasure including the Holy Grail and Ark of the Covenant, Freemason secrets, Marie Antoinette's jewels taken to Nova Scotia, and Francis Bacon as a possible Shakespeare link, with mercury flasks reportedly found. Josh doubts the Bacon-Shakespeare idea.

segments.title: Eldorado Company and nineteenth-century digging
segments.summary: In 1866 the Eldorado Company dug shafts and tunnels and tried to divert water, which destroyed landmarks and made the original pit hard to locate. The oak trees used as guides were cut down. The hosts link this to the California gold rush treasure fever.

segments.title: Twentieth-century expeditions: Dunfield, Triton Alliance, Blankenship, Nolan's Cross
segments.summary: Robert Dunfield built a causeway and dug to about 140 feet in secret until 2003, finding 1600s porcelain and a cavern. Later the Triton Alliance (David Tobias and Dan Blankenship) used an underwater camera in 1970 and claimed to see human remains and treasure. A dispute with Fred Nolan involved a rifle. Nolan's Cross, five cone-shaped boulders, is also mentioned. Blankenship still lives on the island and the Lagina brothers' TV show is discussed.

segments.title: Skeptic wrap-up and the question of evidence
segments.summary: The hosts assess the evidence: the early McGinnis story rests on hearsay since nothing was documented until the nineteenth century, the stone is lost, and the parchment scrap could have been planted to raise funds. Skeptics say the finger drains are weird but not proof of treasure.

segments.title: Listener mail: poison ivy in smoke from firewood
segments.summary: Listener JB writes that as a child, burning poison ivy-tainted logs in a fireplace caused the sap in the smoke to swell her sister's face and throat, requiring an emergency room visit. The hosts comment on the passport photo and sign off with listener contact info.
